title: Europe’s intrinsic strengths in innovation
text:
Europe’s intrinsic strengths in innovation
More than half of the top 25 countries in a world index on innovation are in Europe. A few big factors: social and institutional trust, collaborative research, and policy consistency.
When it comes to investment and growth in artificial intelligence, American firms are undisputed world leaders. But in overall innovation across the global economy, the United States is edged out by two much smaller nations.
In the recently published Global Innovation Index 2026, the 1-2-3 ranking of Switzerland, Sweden, and the U.S. remains unchanged from that of the preceding three years. (Switzerland has occupied the No. 1 spot since 2011, with Sweden and the U.S. occasionally trading places, and with South Korea and Singapore completing the top five in recent years.)
Counter to recent pessimistic assessments of the continent’s innovation and growth potential, European nations occupy 14 of the top 25 spots in this index. This positioning points to perhaps unheralded strengths in Europe’s slower but steadier path, when compared with the high-valuation, high-competition, AI-fueled trajectories of the U.S. and China.
Produced annually by the World Intellectual Property Organization, the index evaluates a range of “inputs” (including human capital, research, institutions, and infrastructure) alongside new knowledge, technologies, and creative outputs produced.
“The [index] ... takes a broad view of human ingenuity and creativity,” The Economist observed last week, noting that innovativeness ranges from “unlocking the scientific mysteries of the universe” to enacting prosaic but “helpful policy reforms.”
According to analysts, Europe’s unique economic characteristics include a balanced “all-rounder” approach, substantial academia-industry-government research collaboration, and regulatory and policy consistency.
Another ingredient – not easily captured by economic data – that supports European innovation appears to be a reservoir of institutional and social trust within and among citizens and their governments. In Sweden, 83% of citizens express trust in fellow citizens, while 62% of Swiss adults trust their national government. In the U.S., 55% of Americans trust each other, while trust in the federal government has reached an all-time low of 27%.
“Sweden is ... one of the most transparent countries in the world and, consequently, one of the most trusting,” business reporter Ben Chapman observed in The Independent several years ago. “Transparency has helped foster an atmosphere of collaboration that has been vital in building new tech companies,” he concluded, with examples that include Klarna, Spotify, and Hexagon.
In a talk on “The Past and Future of Innovation” earlier this year, 2025 Nobel Memorial Prize-winning economist Joel Mokyr alluded to the long-established American values underpinning innovation and economic growth.
A “competitive, open, and free market for ideas” and a governmental approach that is “not too controlling and not too absent” help incentivize firms to “think differently and pursue new ideas,” Dr. Mokyr noted – before going on to add words of caution:
“Self-interest and mistrust, whether in the fields of politics, business or everyday social media interactions, can hamstring scientific exploration and advancement if left unchallenged.”
